Semantic Anarchy · distribution report

What the prompt corpus actually looks like

4,144 prompts, encoded once through SD 1.5's CLIP text encoder, taken apart coordinate by coordinate. The question behind every figure here is the same: where is the leverage for a better sampler? Some of the answers are negative results, and those turned out to be the useful ones.

Generated by scripts/analyze_distribution.py and scripts/build_distribution_report.py. Every number below is read from outputs/analysis/stats.json; every figure is regenerable from the cached corpus.

The short version

Four findings, two of which were surprises

The corpus is globally multimodal, and the single fitted Gaussian averages over that. BIC on the leading components picks k = 30, with a clear interior minimum. The largest split is visible by eye in the PC1–PC2 plane: prompts long enough to fill CLIP's 77-token window form a detached lobe, and PC1 — which correlates 0.69 with prompt length — comes out bimodal rather than bell-shaped.

Per-coordinate sigma modulation has almost nothing to bite on. Ninety-eight per cent of the 59,136 coordinates have a sigma within a factor of 3.0 of each other, and the UNet's sensitivity to them spans only 1.3× — uncorrelated with sigma. The one genuinely frozen group, the BOS row, the fit already reproduces exactly. Freezing, boosting or skewing individual coordinates is not where a better sampler comes from.

The non-Gaussianity that remains is a mixture, not a shape. CLIP pads to 77 with EOS, so at any middle position the corpus is two populations — prompts still carrying content, and prompts already padding. That unmodelled binary explains up to 89% of a coordinate's variance, and it is what makes the widest coordinates bimodal with the fitted Gaussian peaking in the empty gap between the lobes. It is a second, per-position mixture, layered under the global one above.

Coordinate independence fails along exactly one axis. Channels within a token row are nearly independent (0.06); the same channel across rows correlates at 0.66. The diagonal sampler generates 77 mutually unrelated summaries of 77 different prompts and hands them to the model as one tensor — row coherence 0.00 against the corpus's 0.65.

Everything else — per-position energy budgets, the magnitude of variance the model can read, the calibration of the distance gauge — the current implementation gets right. The failure is structural, not scalar.

Measured on xander_prompts_to_encode.txt (4,144 prompts) through juggernaut_reborn.safetensors. Numbers that depend on the corpus's own composition — how long its prompts are, how formulaic they are — are called out as such where they appear, because they are the ones that move when the prompt file changes.

The sequence axis

01Not all 77 token positions are the same object

The conditioning tensor is usually described as "77 tokens of 768 channels", which invites treating the token axis as homogeneous. It is not. Position 0 is the BOS embedding and its variance across all 4,144 prompts is exactly zero — 768 coordinates that are bit-identical in every prompt in the corpus. The fit already handles this correctly: sigma = 0 means the sampler reproduces BOS perfectly without anyone having to pin it. The old implementation's commented-out "restore the real BOS row" trick was solving a problem the per-token fit solves statistically.

The far more surprising half is the padding. CLIP's text encoder is causal, so a row at position 60 has attended to the entire prompt — it is a running summary, not a blank. Everything past the median EOS (position 23) holds 70% of the corpus's total variance. Most of what this distribution encodes lives in the region a naive reading would call filler.

How much of the sequence is padding is a property of the corpus, not of CLIP. This one runs to position 76: a substantial minority of these prompts are long enough to fill the 77-token window outright, so there is no always-padding tail worth naming — the per-position variance share is nearly flat across all 77 positions. A corpus of short tag-style prompts would instead leave a wide, rigid tail. Both regimes matter below, because the sampler's worst structural mismatch (figure 09) lives in exactly that region.

One position is a genuine outlier for shape rather than scale: position 1, which has a mean excess kurtosis of 7 against roughly zero everywhere else. Position 1 is the first content token, so a corpus that reuses a small set of opening words drives that row's marginals nearly categorical — spikes with long tails, not bells.

Per-coordinate sigma

02The sigma landscape is flat — there is nothing to freeze but BOS

This is the figure that tests the "modulate the sigmas per coordinate" idea directly, and the answer is a clean negative. Excluding the BOS row, 98% of coordinates have sigma between 0.57 and 1.72. That is a factor of 3.0 across the entire tensor, where the intuition behind per-coordinate sigma modulation expects orders of magnitude. There is no population of much-wider or much-narrower coordinates waiting to be treated differently.

The participation ratio makes the same point as one number: the corpus's variance is spread over the equivalent of 36,867 equally-weighted coordinates out of 59,136 — 62% of a perfectly uniform budget. Ninety per cent of the variance still needs 85% of the coordinates. Sorted, the landscape is a gentle ramp with exactly one cliff, and that cliff is exactly 768 coordinates wide.

This does not mean the intuition was wrong — it means the leverage is somewhere else. The next three figures find it in the shape of the marginals, and figure 09 finds it in the correlation structure. Neither is visible if you only look at sigma.

Marginal shape

03Mostly Gaussian, with loud exceptions

52% of live coordinates sit inside the band a truly Gaussian coordinate occupies at N=4,144, and a normality test rejects for only a minority at every width. The per-coordinate Gaussian is a reasonable default here, and more than that: the extremes are mild. No coordinate exceeds skew 2.9 or excess kurtosis 16, and only 0.02% fall outside the frame plotted here at all. A smaller, more formulaic corpus produces far wilder shapes; the breadth of this one averages them out.

Two sub-results settle open questions from the algorithm report. First, asymmetry: measuring the spread above and below the mean separately, only 2% of live coordinates are more than 25% lopsided. The original implementation's asymmetric k × [q05, q95] clamp was correcting something real but small — a refinement, not a different regime. A sigma+ / sigma- split sampler is not where the gains are.

Second, truncation. The bulk of coordinates reach a maximum |z| of about 3.76, exactly what 4,144 Gaussian draws should give. But 1.6% go past 5 sigma and 0.08% past 8. Truncating at 2–3 sigma is therefore not a safety rail — it clips behaviour the real corpus exhibits.

Twenty real marginals

04What the coordinates actually look like

Twenty coordinates chosen to span the shape space, each with the Gaussian the diagonal sampler substitutes for it. The middle of the gallery is reassuring: coordinate after coordinate where the orange curve sits neatly on the blue histogram.

The panels drawn from the widest channels are not. Several show two clean lobes with a hole between them, and the fitted Gaussian peaking squarely in the hole. Bimodality here is not a curiosity of a few odd coordinates — it is a property of being a wide channel, which is to say a property of exactly the coordinates that carry the most signal. Figure 05 explains why.

The mixture

05The hidden binary: is this position past the EOS?

CLIP pads to 77 with EOS. For any position in the middle of the prompt-length distribution, the corpus is therefore a mixture of two populations: prompts whose content still reaches this far, and prompts that ended earlier and are now padding. That latent binary is in no fitted model anywhere in this repo, and it is the direct cause of the bimodality in figure 04.

At the most strongly gated coordinate — position 18, channel 324 — that single yes/no explains 89% of the variance. The two lobes sit at +3.9 and -4.9; the fitted Gaussian puts its peak in the gap, and only 59% of real prompts fall within one sigma of that fitted mean where a Gaussian would put 68%. Every diagonal draw near the mean of this coordinate is a value no real prompt ever produced.

Across the tensor, 358 coordinates take more than a quarter of their variance from this one binary and 110 take more than half. The effect switches on around position 4 and off again past 75 — exactly the span of the prompt-length distribution. Outside that window every prompt agrees and the mixture vanishes.

This is the most actionable finding in the report, and the fix needs no new machinery: draw a prompt length first, then sample conditionally on it.

How many axes are real

06Only ~416 of the 4,143 components clear the noise floor

The null here is built by shuffling every coordinate independently across prompts: identical marginals, all correlation destroyed. Where the corpus spectrum drops to meet it is where real structure ends. That happens at component 416, and those axes carry 76% of the corpus's total variance — the rest is real variance with no reliable direction attached to it.

This has a direct consequence for a shipped knob. --comp-lo exists to skip the dominant "tasteful" axes and ride idiosyncratic minor ones. Above component 416 there is nothing idiosyncratic to ride — those axes are sampling error given a direction by a 4,144-row SVD. Set with --equalize, which deliberately amplifies minor axes to full strength, the current defaults can spend the entire deviation budget on estimation noise.

The effective dimensionality tells the positive half of the story: 4,144 prompts buy roughly 113 usable directions, against ~3725 for an independent-coordinate corpus of the same size. That gap is the whole reason the pca sampler works — the corpus is a thin, structured sheet.

The corpus basis

07The rotation that used to fix the marginals no longer does

The pca sampler draws N(0,1) coefficients per axis, and unlike the raw coordinates the corpus scores genuinely justify that. Skew and excess kurtosis sit inside the N=4,144 sampling band from the first axis onward; the whitened radius over the top 200 components lands at 14.0 against the √200 = 14.1 a Gaussian would give.

This is where the corpus overturns an earlier conclusion. Mean absolute excess kurtosis on the raw coordinates is 0.20, and on the leading 416 PCA scores it is 0.30 — the rotation makes the marginals worse, not better. On a corpus of short, formulaic prompts the raw coordinates are strongly bimodal and the change of basis absorbs it. Here the raw coordinates are already close to Gaussian, so there is no artefact left to absorb, and the rotation instead concentrates the corpus's real structure into a few loudly non-Gaussian leading axes.

PC1 is the clearest case: two visibly separate lobes rather than a bell. That is the prompt-length split of figure 08 seen edge-on, and it means the pca sampler's N(0,1) draw on its first axis is putting mass in a gap the corpus leaves empty. From roughly PC3 onward the scores are Gaussian and the assumption holds. The constraint on a better sampler is therefore narrow and specific: fix the first two axes, not the basis.

Global geometry

08Several blobs — and the first axes are prompt length

The original description called for a "mixture of uncorrelated Gaussians", and on this corpus that call was right. BIC on a diagonal GMM over the top 20 components picks k = 30, with a clear interior minimum — not the k = 1 a homogeneous corpus gives. The single Gaussian this repo fits is averaging over genuinely distinct populations of prompt, and it does so on top of the local per-position mixture of figure 05. These are two different mixtures and both are unmodelled.

The PC1–PC2 plane shows the largest of those populations directly: a detached lobe of prompts long enough to fill the whole token window, sitting apart from the main cloud rather than at the end of a gradient. Deeper in, the PC3–PC4 plane is an ordinary elliptical cloud with no clusters, arms or holes — the structure is concentrated in the leading axes, exactly where figure 07 finds the non-Gaussian scores.

Which brings up what those leading axes actually encode. PC1 and PC2 carry |r| = 0.69 and 0.64 with how many words the prompt had; past component ~2 nothing does. The dominant directions the pca sampler starts from are, in substantial part, a prompt-length knob in disguise. Low --comp-lo is not a purely semantic control.

Correlation structure

09Independence fails along exactly one axis — the sequence axis

This is the decomposition that matters most for sampler design. Two channels inside a single token row correlate at a median |r| of 0.055, barely above the 0.010 an independent corpus of this size would show. The diagonal sampler's independence assumption is essentially correct there.

The same channel at two different positions correlates at 0.657. The position × position map shows why: the padding tail is one rigid block, because every row in it is a running summary of the same prompt. Coordinate independence is not uniformly wrong — it is wrong in one specific direction, and that direction happens to hold most of the variance.

Quantified: the mostly-padding tail — the positions that are already padding in more than three-quarters of prompts — spends 33,792 coordinates on about 78 real directions. A diagonal draw hands that block 33,792 independent ones. 57% of the sampler's entropy budget is being poured into a subspace the corpus treats as almost rigid.

Radius

10The corpus is a band; every sampler is a spike

In 59,136 dimensions a Gaussian concentrates onto a razor-thin shell, and the diagonal sampler duly does: relative spread 0.004 against the corpus's 0.032, about 9× tighter. Every diagonal draw sits at the same distance from the centre, which means temperature is the only radial control available — and it is a global one, applied to all draws at once rather than varying between them.

The repo's whitened distance gauge is honestly calibrated (mean 0.99, sd 0.03 on the corpus it was fitted to), but real prompts only ever span 0.89 to 1.11. Everything the taste loop calls "the periphery" — d > 1.3 — is territory no real prompt occupies. That is the point of the exercise, but it is worth naming precisely: it is extrapolation, not a sparsely-visited corner of the corpus.

Both samplers reproduce the corpus's per-position energy budget almost exactly. Whatever is wrong is not a question of scale.

Model sensitivity

11What the UNet can actually read

Conditioning enters SD through exactly two projections per cross-attention block, attn2.to_k and attn2.to_v. A channel's column in those matrices is its only path into the image, so the column norm is a direct, gradient-free first-order sensitivity — no decoding, no probing. (It ignores what attention then does with the keys and values, so read it as a bound on linear leverage, not the full story.)

If some conditioning channels were far more sensitive than others it would show here, and it does not. Between the 1st and 99th percentile the whole range spans 1.3×, and sensitivity correlates with corpus sigma at r = +0.18 — a cloud, not a trend. Combining the two, 594 of 768 channels carry 80% of the effective drive where a perfectly flat budget would need 614. Selecting or freezing channels is not where a better sampler comes from.

The last panel is the sharper test. Projecting the true channel covariance through each of the 32 matrices and comparing against what the diagonal model claims, the ratio stays inside 0.78–1.54. The diagonal model gets the magnitude of readable variance right to about 20%. Taken with figure 10, this settles the diagnosis: the magnitudes are right everywhere, and the failure is that the 77 rows it hands the model do not agree with one another.

Scoreboard

12What each shipped sampler actually produces

512 draws from every sampler, measured against the corpus on the statistics above. Real prompts sit at a nearest-neighbour cosine of 0.61 from each other. Diagonal draws sit at 0.25 — further from every real prompt than any real prompt is from any other. Hybrid at 0.84 is the opposite failure, near-copies. pca at 0.41 is the only sampler in between, and even it does not reach the corpus.

The clearest single line is position-to-position coherence. The corpus's 77 rows move together at 0.65; the diagonal sampler's move at 0.00. It is generating 77 mutually unrelated summaries of 77 different prompts and handing them to the model as one conditioning tensor. pca (0.65) and hybrid (0.63) recover it; blend at coherence 0.5 lands at 0.32, midway, exactly as its covariance interpolation predicts.

One property no parametric sampler reproduces: marginal shape. The corpus carries mean |excess kurtosis| 0.28; diagonal, pca and blend all flatten to 0.17. The gap is real but narrow on this corpus — its raw marginals are close to Gaussian to begin with (figure 03) — so of the implications below, this is the one whose payoff has shrunk the most. Whether it matters for image quality is an open question this analysis cannot settle.

What follows from it

Eight implications for the sampler

These are implications, not tested results — the analysis measures the corpus, not the images. They are ordered by how much of the measured mismatch each one would close.

1. Sample a prompt length, then condition on it

figure 05

The single largest modelling gap. 358 coordinates take >25% of their variance from a binary nobody models. Fit the distribution twice per position — once for "content", once for "padding" — draw a length from the corpus's own length histogram, and the bimodality of figure 04 disappears. This is a change to fit and sample, not a new sampler.

2. Fix cross-position coherence, not per-coordinate sigma

figures 02, 09, 12

The diagonal sampler is right about channels within a row (0.055) and wrong about the same channel across rows (0.657). A "row-coherent diagonal" — draw one per-channel deviation and share it across positions with a per-position modulation — would keep the anarchy of independent channels while restoring the structure that actually matters. The measured correlation is itself the mixing weight: devt = √ρ u + √(1−ρ) vt with ρ ≈ 0.66 (u shared across positions, vt fresh per row, both scaled by the per-coordinate sigma) reproduces the marginal variances exactly and the cross-position correlation to first order. Note the old implementation's mix_latents row crossover is not this operator: it copies each row from a different parent, which keeps every row internally real but scrambles the sequence axis in the same way the diagonal sampler does. The row-coherent piece exists in neither codebase.

3. Cap --comp-lo at ~416

figure 06

Above that, the axes are sampling noise. Combined with --equalize, which amplifies minor axes to full strength, the current ranges can spend the whole deviation budget on estimation error. A hard cap costs nothing and removes a knob range that cannot work.

4. Draw the first two PCA axes from the corpus, not from N(0,1)

figures 07, 08

PC1 is two lobes, not a bell, because it is prompt length in disguise — and the pca sampler puts N(0,1) mass squarely in the gap between them. From PC3 onward the Gaussian assumption is fine. Sampling the leading one or two coefficients from their own empirical CDF (or jointly with the drawn prompt length above, which is the same variable) fixes the whole effect for the cost of two sorted arrays.

5. Reproduce the remaining marginals with a rank transform

figures 07, 12

The same copula-style step generalises: sample in PCA space as now, then push each coordinate through its own empirical CDF. Marginal shape comes back exactly and the correlation structure is untouched. Ranked lower than it once was — on this corpus the raw marginals are already close to Gaussian, so the gap being closed (0.28 against 0.17) is modest.

6. Give the radius its own distribution

figures 10, 12

The corpus is a band of radii (relative spread 0.032); every sampler is a spike. retarget() already pins a sample's distance to a chosen value — draw that target from the corpus's own distance distribution instead of a constant, and the population matches rather than a single shell.

7. Do not expect gains from channel selection or sigma reshaping

figures 02, 11

Sigma spans 3.0× across the tensor, UNet sensitivity spans 1.3×, and the two are uncorrelated (r = +0.18). Freezing, boosting or skewing individual coordinates has almost nothing to bite on. The one coordinate group that is genuinely frozen — the BOS row — the fit already handles exactly, at sigma = 0.

8. Loosen truncation, or drop it

figure 03

1.6% of coordinates reach past 5 sigma in the real corpus and 0.08% past 8. Truncating at 2–3 sigma removes behaviour the corpus exhibits rather than preventing blow-outs. If a clamp is wanted, the original implementation's empirical k × [q05, q95] envelope respects the actual marginals; a symmetric z-clip does not.

Control

Is any of this a property of the finetune?

Everything above is measured through juggernaut_reborn.safetensors, which is an SD 1.5 finetune — and a finetune that touched the text encoder: 196 of its 197 CLIP tensors differ from base SD 1.5, by up to 1% of each tensor's own magnitude. Since the corpus is the text encoder's output, that is enough to worry about. So the entire analysis was re-run on the same 4,144 prompts through stock v1-5-pruned-emaonly.safetensors, changing nothing else.

1 of the 22 headline numbers moves materially (more than 10% relatively, or 0.05 absolute for the quantities already expressed as fractions or correlations): coordinates with eta² > 0.25. Everything else — every correlation, every effective-dimension count, the whole sampler scoreboard — is unchanged to the digits printed here. The report's conclusions are properties of the prompts and of CLIP's architecture, not of this finetune.

The one number that does move is a count sitting on a threshold: how many coordinates take more than a quarter of their variance from the past-EOS switch. v1-5-pruned-emaonly.safetensors puts more coordinates just over that line. The underlying effect is the same size in both — the most gated coordinate is at eta² 0.89 vs 0.90 — so this is threshold sensitivity, not a different phenomenon.

Read the table as a robustness check on the report, not as a comparison of model quality. Nothing here says which checkpoint makes better images; it says only that the shape of the conditioning distribution survives the finetune. Note also what this does not cover: the figures themselves are still rendered from the primary checkpoint, and the base-checkpoint set is on disk under outputs/analysis_base/plots/ rather than inlined here, to keep the page to one download.
